utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon to Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. There are a few matters which I would like to briefly address. The first one is the following: Mr. Tieger, if you would like to make any observations, express any concerns about the use of Rule 84 bis, then you're invited to do so at the end of -- so not prior to the beginning of Mr. Krajisnik to make a statement, but at the end of your submissions in the context of the closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We understood that, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Will I briefly be able to introduce that by explaining where we're up to at the relevant time, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then also at that time. I'd rather not mix up all these things. Procedural debates is one and hearing a statement is another matter. I think that it's then up to the Prosecution to start second round of final argument. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. In respect of the answers to the questions put to the Prosecution by the Chamber, Mr. Gaynor will make the submissions on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The first question Your Honours asked was, assuming that we, the Office of the Prosecutor, have proved what we say we've proved, why wouldn't conviction in this case, based on a combination of instigation and aiding and abetting, be the correct result? There are two issues in Your Honours' question, and I will address both briefly. The first issue is whether, on any one count, the Chamber can enter a finding of instigating and aiding and abetting in respect of the same acts. The jurisprudence on this point is not yet settled. I refer Your Honours to the separate opinions of Judge Schomburg and Shahabuddeen attached to the Kamuhanda appeal judgement of 19 September 2005. Judge Schomburg suggests that a conviction naming two or more forms of liability under Article 7.1 of the Statute on the same count in respect of the same acts may be impermissibly cumulative. Judge Shahabuddeen, with whom Judge Weinberg de Roca agreed, opined that such convictions are not impermissibly cumulative. The judgement itself does not contain a substantive discussion of this issue. The second issue is whether in this case a combination of instigation and aiding and abetting would be the correct result. In our submission, neither mode of liability, whether taken separately or together in respect of any particular count, fully encompasses the criminal conduct and intent of the accused in this case. I will deal with each mode of liability separately. I will deal first with aiding and abetting. Tribunal jurisprudence recognises that aiding and abetting is usually considered to incur a lesser degree of individual criminal responsibility than participation in a joint criminal enterprise. I refer to the Vasiljevic appeal judgement, paragraph 102, and the Milutinovic decision of the Appeals Chamber of the 21st of May, 2003, at paragraph 20. An aider and abettor carries out acts that assist, encourage, or lends moral support to the perpetration of a crime, and this support has a substantial effect upon the perpetration of the crime. The requisite mental element is knowledge that the acts performed by the aider and abettor assist the commission of the crime. In this case, Mr. Krajisnik did much more than merely assisting, encouraging or lending moral support to others. A group of persons, including Mr. Krajisnik, acting jointly, designed and orchestrated the implementation of a massive criminal campaign to achieve the purpose of physically removing Muslims and Croats from the targeted territory by any means necessary, including the crimes charged in the indictment. The size of the campaign meant that it could not be carried out by any one person, and necessarily required the contributions of many. The characterisation of the accused's guilt must reflect this reality. Krajisnik was not acting alone, and he was such a central participant that it would be inappropriate to characterise the crimes committed as someone else's crimes which he aided or abetted. As the Appeals Chamber in Tadic said, common purpose liability is "not only dictated by the object and purpose of the Statute but is also warranted by the very nature of many international crimes which are committed most commonly in wartime situations. Most of the time these crimes do not result from the criminal propensity of single individuals but constitute manifestations of collective criminality: The crimes are often carried out by groups of individuals acting in pursuance of a common criminal design." That's the Tadic appeal judgement, at paragraph 191. I will now address instigating. To instigate is to prompt another person to commit an act or omission with the awareness of the substantial likelihood that a crime will be committed in the execution of that instigation. In our submission, the evidence is sufficient to support a conviction for instigation in each count in this case. I simply add that there is a suggestion in the Gacumbitsi appeal judgement of the 7th of July, 2006, at paragraph 61, based on the facts in that case but possibly of more general application, that instigating may carry a lower degree of seriousness as a mode of liability than committing. We submit that, while instigating is more reflective of the accused's responsibility than aiding and abetting, instigating may still not be fully reflective of the depth and breadth of the accused's criminal participation in the crimes alleged. In respect of question 2, I addressed questions 2(A) and 2(B) in my submissions to you on Tuesday. In question 2(C) you asked whether, if the accused had effective control over persons or groups that committed crimes, why do you not ask the Chamber to declare the accused responsible under Article 7.3 of the Statute in relation to those crimes; or if Article 7.1 is insisted upon, for ordering the commission of the crimes? I will deal with Article 7.3 first. First, as a matter of clarification, allegations under 7.3 in the indictment have not been withdrawn and remain in place. The evidence in this case supports a conviction for superior responsibility for each count. There are a number of reasons why we did not emphasise 7.3 liability in our brief. As Your Honours are no doubt aware, the Chamber cannot enter convictions under 7.1 and 7.3 for the same conduct in respect of any particular count, as this would be impermissibly cumulative. I refer to the Blaskic appeal judgement, paragraph 92. Where the legal requirements of both 7.1 and 7.3 forms of responsibility are met, a conviction should be entered on the basis of Article 7.1 only, and the Chamber should consider the accused's superior position as an aggravating factor in sentencing. I refer to the Kvocka appeal judgement, paragraph 104, and the Blaskic appeal judgement, paragraph 91. There are three specific reasons why we do not focus on Article 7.3 liability in our brief. First, as we have argued, the accused and Karadzic were at the apex of the Bosnian Serb campaign to remove non-Serbs from target territories, and actively participated in the preparation for and implementation of that campaign. It would be an inaccurate characterisation of criminal liability to enter a conviction for the co-architect of a massive campaign of great brutality for merely failing to prevent or punish crimes which he intended, and it would be an understatement of the depth and breadth of Mr. Krajisnik's participation in the crimes alleged. Second, in our submission, it would be against elementary considerations of justice and the spirit of the Statute, which seeks to hold accountable those most responsible for massive crimes, to convict a mere foot soldier or policeman who committed murder in pursuit of the criminal campaign of the Bosnian Serb leadership under Article 7.1, yet to convict one of the masterminds of that campaign under Article 7.3. Third, the indictment in this case does not allege that the accused had superior responsibility over all forces who committed crimes in pursuit of the aim to forcibly remove non-Serbs from target areas of Bosnia. Those crimes are encompassed by JCE liability but would not fall within a 7.3 conviction. A 7.3 conviction would therefore, in our submission, fail to reflect the responsibility of the accused for crimes committed in pursuit of the objective of ethnic separation by forces with whom he worked in concert but over which he did not have effective control. For these three reasons, we submit that a 7.3 conviction on any one count, while supported by the evidence, would not properly reflect the degree of the accused's participation in the crimes alleged. In question 2(C), Your Honours also asked why we did not ask the Chamber to declare the accused responsible for ordering the commission of crimes. We maintain the allegations in the indictment that the accused is liable for ordering the crimes. The evidence supports a conviction for ordering in respect of each count in the indictment. As a general proposition, ordering would be an appropriate mode of liability on which to enter a conviction on this case. We note, however, that we did not allege that the accused was in a position of authority in respect of some forces, in particular JNA personnel committing crimes in pursuit of the objective of forcible ethnic separation prior to the establishment of the VRS on the 12th of May, 1992. The relationship between the JNA and the Bosnian Serb leadership prior to the establishment of the VRS was one of cooperation rather than ordering. The Court may, therefore, in the exercise of its discretion, conclude that the accused is not liable for ordering the JNA and instead acted in cooperation with the JNA to implement the objective of the criminal plan. This form of liability would be very accurately reflected in a JCE conviction. Now, in question 2(D), you said, alternatively, if our use of terms suggestive of effective control in our final trial brief meant to allege that the accused -- that while the accused himself might not have had effective control over certain or any persons or groups committing alleged crimes, other people in the same JCE of which the accused was a member had effective control over those groups and persons. It is correct that persons in the same JCE as Krajisnik had effective control over certain groups. By way of example, Kukanjac had effective control over JNA soldiers in the 2nd Military District. The correct mode of liability to reflect the accused's responsibility for crimes committed by forces over which another JCE member had effective control is, we submit, joint criminal enterprise. If the Chamber were to find the accused to be a member of a JCE consisting of a core group, he would be liable for the acts of subordinates of other JCE members when carried out pursuant to the JCE. Question 3, I won't read out the entire question. Your Honours identify a number of references in the brief where we describe, for example, Plavsic and Koljevic as marginalised or relatively marginal, with Djeric and a government who were weak, totally subservient, and you ask whether we are implying that some members of the alleged JCE were merely peripheral or powerless, having made much lesser contributions, whereas others were core members who bear responsibility for all the crimes committed. Is it, in other words, you asked, your position that membership of a JCE does not necessarily make each member responsible, or equally responsible, for all the crimes committed pursuit to the JCE? You asked for authorities in support of our submissions. Now, in respect of question 3(A), our answer is that each member of the JCE who shared the intent to pursue the common purpose of the JCE and made a contribution to it, is criminally liable for the crimes committed in furtherance of the common purpose. As I mentioned in my earlier submissions, there is no specific legal requirement that an accused make a substantial contribution to a JCE. Support for that is the Kvocka appeal judgement at paragraph 96. It might be paragraph 97, actually. Now, it is our position that certain JCE participants made greater contributions than others. This fact was publicly acknowledged by the Prosecution in the factual basis in the Plavsic case, which was accepted by the Trial Chamber in that case. The use in our final brief of terms such as "marginalised" and "subservient" and "sidelined" are to be understood stood in the sense that certain individuals were marginalised or sidelined in respect of the inner core of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Some of the participants who made lesser contributions to the JCE, such as Djeric or Subotic, still made significant contributions to the JCE. The extent of participation of an accused in a JCE is a factor which may be taken into account in determining sentence. Now, our authorities are three: First of all, the Stakic appeal judgement at paragraph 380, where the Appeals Chamber, having found that Stakic was a participant in a JCE, went on to find that his role in the commission of the crimes underlying the common purpose was by no means criminal -- was by no means minimal. Correction. In the Kvocka appeal judgement, the Appeals Chamber examined the individual participation of a number of accused who were involved in the JCE to run the Omarska camp in order to determine sentence. In the Babic appeals judgement, at paragraph 40, the Chamber recognised that a Chamber may, in its discretion, assess the participation of the accused in a JCE relative to the participation of others when determining sentence. Your Honours' question 4 concerned JCE 2. You pointed out that JCE 2 was not dealt with at the 98 bis stage in this case. You asked us to explain why would it be wrong of the Chamber to hold that, even if this had been a live option prior to that point, it is no longer an allegation that may fairly be considered. The Trial Chamber may, in its discretion, decide to apply or not to apply JCE 2. The JCE in the indictment in this case was pleaded in accordance with the jurisprudence which applies to the pleading of joint criminal enterprise liability. Further, the facts from which the mens rea for JCE 2 participation may be inferred were pleaded in the indictment. It is clear from the indictment that it is alleged that Mr. Krajisnik had knowledge of a criminal system designed to remove Muslims and Croats from the indictment municipalities and also intent to further that system. We acknowledge, however, that JCE 2 was not dealt with at the 98 bis stage and it is a matter of discretion as to whether the Trial Chamber wishes to apply JCE 2 liability. It would not be wrong not to apply it. Question 5, Your Honours asked us to identified which is the first in time charged crime committed pursuant to the alleged JCE, including the accused. You asked: Who were the members of the JCE at this point? The first charged crime committed pursuant to the JCE is scheduled incident 1.1 in schedule A, which is the killing of at least 48 Bosnian Muslim and/or Bosnian Croat men, women and children in the town of Bijeljina on the 1st or 2nd of April. It's actually -- in the indictment, it's 1-2 April, 1992. Now, while I'm on the subject of the Bijeljina, I wish to make one correction to the Prosecution's final brief. I refer Your Honours to paragraph 246 of our brief. Now, at the end of the paragraph which is at the first bullet point, you see a reference to President Micic. I would like to invite Your Honours to strike that and insert the word "Novakovic." Now, as Mr. Stewart pointed out yesterday, the reference to Micic at paragraph 246 of our brief, which Mr. Harmon referred to at page 27301 of his submissions, of the transcript of this case, was a mistake. It was Novakovic who spoke to Mr. Krajisnik, according to the accused's own evidence at transcript page 24298. The incident, this telephone call, is also referred to at paragraph 333 of our brief, which correctly refers to Novakovic. I also wish to note a somewhat more substantive point. Mr. Stewart stated yesterday in the course of referring to paragraph 246 of our brief, that, "Mr. Krajisnik didn't talk to Mauzer." That, in our submission, is not correct. I refer Your Honours to the transcript of the evidence of Mr. Krajisnik, page 24298, referred to at footnote 631 of our brief. I will simply read out the relevant lines of that page, which are lines 9 to 15, to clarify the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, would you have the day as well? Because for me it's difficult to -- in my LiveNote I find dates --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the 18th of May, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 18th of May. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. I will read the relevant passage, Your Honours. "I was in the offices or cabinet of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this man's name was Mr. Novakovic, and I asked him what was going on. And he said: I can't tell you over the phone, and somebody snatched the receiver away from him, and I heard the voice of a man who says: "While you're sitting down over there, we're doing your work for you. And who was that? That was Mr. Mauzer." Now, I'm going to move on from that point, Your Honours. Your Honours asked who were the JCE members at the time of the first charged crimes. As pleaded in our indictment, the objective of the joint criminal enterprise was the permanent removal by force or other means of Bosnian Muslim, Bosnian Croat, or other non-Serb inhabitants from large areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina through the commission of crimes punishable under the Statute of the Tribunal. It was a vast criminal enterprise, and, like any vast criminal enterprise, its membership was not static. The members of the JCE participated in different ways, in different geographical areas, with the shared intent to secure the objective of forcibly removing non-Serbs from the targeted territory across great parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the end of March 1992, and at the time of the first crimes charged in the indictment, the joint criminal enterprise already included a great number of individuals, including Krajisnik, Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, Arkan, Milosevic, Mauzer, Mico Stanisic, Mandic, Brdjanin, and Kukanjac. It also included those Serb Crisis Staffs which had been established, members of the RS MUP, the Serb TO, and paramilitary groups and JNA personnel. Your Honours may ask why Mladic is not in that list. Mladic and other VRS staff became part of the joint criminal enterprise on the 12th of May, 1992, on the establishment of the VRS. I move now to question 6, which is the specific question about Glogova. You asked: Was the alleged attack on Glogova an action of the alleged joint criminal enterprise, including the accused? If so, explain why, taking into account that neither Karadzic nor Mladic seem to have known about it until after the fact, and Djeric seems to have been displeased with it. The attack was an action of the JCE, including the accused. Bratunac municipality was a municipality with a Muslim majority population, and it was contiguous with Serbia. As such, it was vital to the realisation of Strategic Objective number 3. The nature of the acts committed during the attack on Glogova, which was consistent and contemporaneous with attacks elsewhere in the targeted territory, the forces participating in the attack, the high-level approvals obtained in advance of the attack, the disarmament operation which preceded the attack, and the absence of any effort to hold to account those responsible for the attack are some elements which confirm the view that the attack on Glogova was carried out in pursuit of the campaign to eliminate non-Serbs from the targeted territories. Your Honours have asked a specific question, so I would like to point to specific elements of what I've just outlined. In particular, the evidence shows that the attack on Glogova was intended as part of the plan to create Serbian territory in the Bratunac municipality by forcibly removing its Muslim population. Attacks on and the ethnic cleansing of the Muslim settlements of Suha and Voljevica followed. The features of the attack on Glogova - disarming the village, attacking it, razing the houses and mosque, ethnically cleansing its population, separating the men, beating and killing them, and then forcibly removing them from the municipality - mirrored the pattern of attacks on Muslim settlements that had occurred previously in municipalities that were contiguous with Serbia or otherwise were territories vital for the realisation of Strategic Objective number 3. I refer specifically to the municipalities of Bijeljina, Foca, Zvornik, Visegrad, and Vlasenica. Elsewhere in Bosnia, the same pattern of attacks had occurred in the municipalities of Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa, Brcko, Prijedor and Doboj. The plan to attack Glogova was undertaken with the understanding that it had the approval of the top leadership of the Republika Srpska and Serbia. The operational planning for the attack on Glogova was prepared by the JNA. The decision to attack at Glogova, burn part of the village and forcibly remove its population, as well as ethnically cleanse other Muslim settlements, was formally taken by the Bratunac Crisis Staff at a meeting attended by representatives of the JNA, Serbian state security, the commander of the TO, and the chief of police. The attack on the village was a coordinated, joint operation. The attacking forces consisted of members of the JNA, the TO, the police and "volunteers" from Serbia. The volunteers who participated in the attack had been escorted from Serbia to Bosnia by Goran Zekic, who was a member of the Bosnian Serb Assembly and the SDS main board; Miodrag Jokic, who was vice-president of the Srebrenica SDS; Miroslav Deronjic, who was the Crisis Staff president in Bratunac, and the Serbian police. According to Zekic, the volunteers and the JNA operated pursuant to an agreement between the leadership of Serbia and the leadership of Republika Srpska. The attack on Glogova resulted in the deaths of 65 Muslims, the burning of a significant part of the village, the forcible expulsion of its entire Muslim population, the detention of the men, and the destruction of its sole mosque. Similar attacks, as I pointed out earlier, followed immediately on other Muslim settlements. Muslim men from those settlements, and Glogova, were detained in detention facilities where, as mentioned, they were beaten, killed, and forcibly removed from the municipality. After the attack Deronjic was summoned to Pale where he and other presidents of Bosnian Serb Crisis Staff reported to Mladic, Karadzic, and Ostojic on the military situation in the field. Maps of Bosnia depicting the ethnic composition of municipalities were behind them, with Serb territories marked in blue and Muslim territories in green. Deronjic described in detail the ethnic cleansing that had occurred and was continuing in Bratunac. Following Deronjic's presentation, Ostojic remarked, "Now the municipality of Bratunac can be painted blue." There is no evidence that Deronjic did not know -- correction: There is no evidence that Karadzic did not know about the events in Bratunac prior to this meeting. At the time of the briefing, Mladic had not yet been appointed the head of the Main Staff and was receiving a briefing on the military events in the field. Two days later, at the 16th session, he was formally appointed head of the VRS Main Staff. The evidence does not disclose the reason why Djeric expressed displeasure about the attack on Glogova. The evidence does show that when Muslims, who had been ethnically cleansed from Bratunac, arrived in Pale days later, Djeric was aware of their arrival and provided material assistance to efforts that resulted in their removal from Bosnian Serb territory. Deronjic was never criticised by Karadzic, Mladic, or Ostojic for the actions he described in his oral report. Deronjic was never prosecuted or punished for the attacks on Glogova by the Bosnian Serb authorities. Rather, he later was appointed to the SDS main board and became a vice-president of the SDS. In summary, the evidence establishes that the attack on Glogova was a classic example of an operation of the JCE that fully achieved its objectives. I move now to question number 7. Your Honours quoted two paragraphs from our brief, paragraph 225, and Your Honours quoted a section which reads "especially in April and May, some Crisis Staffs," and you asked: Is it the OTP's theory that only some Crisis Staffs were part of the alleged JCE? Our answer is that all Serb Crisis Staffs were part of the JCE. Paragraph 225 of our brief refers to Crisis Staffs issuing orders to military units and having close contact with the VRS, such as personal contact with Mladic. That's at paragraph 230. Those paragraphs are not tantamount to a position that some Crisis Staffs were outside the JCE, but rather, discusses the relationship between the military and some individual Crisis Staffs. The Hanson report. The Hanson report addresses the issue of military authority of Crisis Staffs with great care. Some Crisis Staffs, especially in April and in May, before the establishment of the VRS, did command local armed units. In other areas, the Crisis Staffs did not command local -- did not command armed units because the JNA was present or the local TO had a robust command structure already in place. The overall pattern, however, is that all Crisis Staffs, at a minimum, supported and coordinated with the Serb armed forces in their municipalities, providing resources and recruits which facilitated the operation of those armed units. All Crisis Staffs acted in support of the operation to achieve the objective of the JCE, because they were established and maintained by the Bosnian Serb leadership through Variant A and B and the Djeric order of 26th April, 1992, precisely in order to seize and maintain power at the municipal level on the claimed territory. Even those Crisis Staffs that may have had little role in commanding local armed forces participated in the persecutory campaign by overseeing the forcible removal of non-Serbs and ordering discriminatory measures against non-Serbs. Question 8 is a relatively long question, but for the record I think I should read it out. Your question was: "What kinds of evidence distinguish Crisis Staffs (and more generally perpetrators of crimes) who were acting as part of the alleged JCE, from those who were not part of the JCE but who were engaged in copycat, or parallel, or independent activities, war crimes per se (relating to fighting a civil war as opposed to pursuant to the alleged JCE objective), or common thuggery arising from the collapse of law and order? First, the evidence does not reveal that there was a collapse of law and order but that the collapse of law and order was partial and discriminatory. Second, the evidence supports the conclusion that all Crisis Staffs were acting as part of the JCE. There is no reliable evidence that there were copycat or independent Crisis Staffs. In respect of what kinds of evidence determine whether a particular Crisis Staff was acting as part of the JCE, we submit that the Court should consider the following non-exhaustive list of factors: How the Crisis Staff was created and who created it; the general composition of the Crisis Staff, including whether it contained individuals holding positions of authority, such as SJB chiefs, TO heads, VRS personnel, or SDS representatives; the relationship of the Crisis Staff members to members who were in the JCE; expressions of intent by Crisis Staff members consistent with the common purpose; evidence of communication from JCE members to the Crisis Staff; evidence of other actions by the Crisis Staff consistent with the objectives of the JCE, including crimes against Muslims and Croats and their property; evidence of acceptance of instructions to the Crisis Staff from JCE members; the pattern of the establishment of Crisis Staffs by the Bosnian Serb leadership. Many of these evidential inquiries may also apply to perpetrators generally, and a non-exhaustive list would also include the following: Whether the perpetrator was a member of, or associated with, any organised bodies connected to the JCE; whether the crimes committed were consistent with the pattern of similar crimes by JCE members against similar kinds of victims; whether the perpetrator acted at the same time as members of the JCE, or as persons who were tools or instruments of the JCE; whether the perpetrator's act advanced the objective of the JCE; whether the perpetrator's act was ratified implicitly or explicitly by members of the JCE; whether the perpetrator acted in cooperation or conjunction with members of the JCE at any relevant time; whether any meaningful effort was made to punish the act by any member of the JCE in a position to do so; whether similar acts were punished by JCE members in a position to do so; whether members of the JCE or those who were tools of the JCE continued to affiliate with the perpetrators after the act; finally - and this is a non-exhaustive list - whether the acts were performed in the context of a systematic attack, including one of relatively low intensity over a long period. In examining the evidence concerning crimes generally, we submit that Your Honours will find that, insofar as any of the criminal incidents proven went beyond what was intended by the accused, we submit that the Chamber should find that, first, it was foreseeable that such crimes might be perpetrated by one or other members of the group; and, second, the accused willingly took that risk, that is, he was aware that such crime was a possible consequence of the execution of the enterprise, and with that awareness, the accused decided to participate in the enterprise. The foreseeability of those crimes has to be assessed in the light of a number of factors. I'll name just four categories. First, evidence that there was a systematic arming of the Serb population and a deliberate campaign to disarm Muslims and Croats. Second, evidence that the Bosnian Serb leadership created and encouraged a culture of impunity in respect of crimes against non-Serbs committed by MUP, VRS, and paramilitary forces, while continuing to enforce the law against Serbs committing crimes, even some relatively minor crimes, against fellow Serbs. Third, evidence that Bosnian Serb leadership was conducting systematic persecutions through the crimes in the indictment. Fourth, evidence that the Bosnian Serb leadership promoted and implemented a propaganda campaign. The leadership instilled in the Serb population of Bosnia-Herzegovina ethnic hatred and fear of annihilation at the hands of Muslims and Croats. Concepts of brotherhood, unity and interethnic tolerance were deliberately debased and discredited. Muslims and Croats were vilified and dehumanised. In this environment of a systematic campaign, whipped-up ethnic hatred, an armed Serb population, a disarmed non-Serb population, and a deliberately created culture of impunity in respect of crimes against non-Serbs, such opportunistic crimes against non-Serbs in the indictment municipalities as did happen were reasonably foreseeable, and the accused was aware that such crimes were a possible consequence of the execution of the joint criminal enterprise. Question 9 is Your Honours' final question. Mr. Tieger answered that on Tuesday, and I now propose to hand over to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. I was informed that most likely the Prosecution would stay within the hour announced, and that means that you have only little to add to that, because you're close to the hour. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me add to that, that using less words doesn't mean that you're saying anything less important. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then I'm sure what I have to say is extremely important, Your Honour. Just a few remarks about the proposed statement. As the Court, I'm sure, is aware the concept of the last word is rather foreign to practitioners from the common law system and quite familiar to those in the civil law system. In our hybrid system here, its incorporation via 84 bis must be understood, in our submission, in light of the requirement under Rule 85 that testimony be taken under oath and subject to cross-examination. It is not intended, in our submission, to be a circumvention of cross-examination or another bite at the apple. And to the extent it is so, it should be accorded no weight. I note, for example, that the accused in Limaj, after testifying, sought to make such a statement and was denied for that reason. Here, the accused has testified to what may, indeed, be an unprecedented degree, certainly over a long period of time. Nevertheless, Your Honour, in this case, the Chamber may well wish to hear from Mr. Krajisnik, and we have advised the Defence accordingly that we do not seek to prevent the Court from doing so, with the exception of three small references that we brought to their attention. And that's our position, subject to the comments I've just offered the Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Before we continue, I would have one question, Mr. Gaynor, on a matter you said. I'll just try to find out whether I understood you well. When you were referring to this paragraph -- let me just find it. I think it was -- yes, 246. You said it's true that Mr. Krajisnik did not speak to Mr. Micic but to Mr. Novakovic, and you said he also talked to Mauzer, and then you referred to -- you read a portion of page 23298.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the page I read from was 24298.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I said that. That's the page I've got in front of me. You read it to us. If I would tell in my own words what happens there, it's that Mr. Krajisnik is in a telephone conversation with Mr. Novakovic; that someone then grabs the telephone, utters a few words; and that afterwards, that person, identified by Mr. Krajisnik as Mr. Mauzer, interrupted the telephone conversation, put down the receiver so that ends the telephone conversation. In your view, talking to is not having a conversation with someone but is just to hear the words of someone who interferes in a telephone conversation you have with someone else. Is that how I have to understand it? If I really start a close reading, then if you would defend this position, I think that your line in 246 should have been, that same day Krajisnik called to the Bijeljina Crisis Staff and Mr. Mauzer talked to him, because I do not see any words in response to what Mr. Mauzer said here. Or am I wrong? Because you use this -- you said, he talked to Mauzer because that's what Mr. Krajisnik said. What Mr. Krajisnik said doesn't give me the impression that there was a conversation. And usually if I say I talked to this and this person, I'm usually referring to having a conversation with someone and not just hearing words uttered by someone or yelling at a distance to someone. I'm just trying to understand whether there's more to understand or whether this is what you wanted to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thanks for the opportunity to clarify it, Your Honour. That is correct. According to that page of the transcript, it is clear that Mr. Mauzer spoke to Mr. Krajisnik, and there is no evidence that Mr. Krajisnik replied in any way. So I take your point, Your Honour. Thanks for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Then I think we'll move on. Mr. Stewart and Mr. Josse, would you prefer to start now or have a break first? We might get a bit in trouble if we do not start now. But it also depends on how much time you think you'd use for final argument, second round.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we shan't exceed the time that the Court had in mind, and I doubt whether we should come that close to it. But, Your Honour, we would appreciate a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just see. If we have a break now, we will resume at 4. Yes, I think it's manageable. So we do not have problems, then, with tapes and forced other breaks. We'll then have a break now for 25 minutes. We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, one of the reasons for asking for the break then was that I wanted to take the opportunity of discussing with my co-counsel, Mr. Josse, his reaction to the way in which matters have proceeded over the last two or three days and this afternoon, because I find it always valuable to see whether and to what extent Mr. Josse and I are ad idem on such matters. We often find we are. We certainly do, for what its worth, on this occasion. Your Honour, what has happened is extremely unsatisfactory. The Prosecution, having had their application to more than double the word length of their final brief from 60.000 to 125.000 words, having had that application refused - it was opposed, it was completely refused, there was no extension - we then had the allocation of basically one day to the Prosecution, one day to the Defence. The Prosecution in a very brisk and efficient manner, in one sense, then managed to rattle through 101 pages, or something like that, of transcript so that they were able to add as much as possible by way of written transcript to the 60.000, or nearly 60.000 words in their final brief. Well, all right. So far so legitimately tactical in the circumstances. No major protest about that. It's clear that we don't really like it, but, all right, we've lived with that. But what they didn't do, as they rattled through like a -- sometimes like a very slickly presented American news programme, with yielding the floor to each other and so on, very efficient and slick, but what they didn't do then was get round, except in relation to one or two questions, get round to dealing with a list of not always easy, not always straightforward, questions which had been supplied by the Trial Chamber last week, at the end of last week. Didn't get round to it. Yesterday evening, we were given the clearest indication that the Prosecution expected to come comfortably within the one-hour allocation. Of course by that time we realised that if they were going to deal with these questions at all, it would have to be today because they hadn't dealt with them. So that was clear. They have in fact taken nearly the full hour, and nearly all of the time that was taken has been taken by Mr. Gaynor dealing with those outstanding questions, and dealing with them both by going to the point of the question, though occasionally not, in fact, going to the point of the question, but also by using today to give the Court, on the transcript, part 3 of their final brief. Part 1, the 59.000 and something words, whatever it was; part 2, the 101 pages of transcript; and part 3, what we got this afternoon. Your Honour, in the course of this case, because of the procedures that are adopted, on many occasions, matters which in the culture with which we on the Defence side as counsel are mainly familiar, but we have to live with the culture we have here, lots and lots of things have had to be dealt with by filing paper, putting in motions, et cetera, et cetera, where we would have felt far more comfortable, and we humbly suggest it might have been a lot more efficient, if there'd just been a quick exchange in court, with everybody making clear what their points of view were, following up with difficulties and it could have all been done and dusted. And then, by contrast, we get this situation where complicated questions are dealt with in this way, and instead of something which, within the proper procedures of this court, does really lend itself to full written submissions, with proper notice and the proper opportunity to consider them and the proper opportunity to deal with them, it's all done orally on the hoof, on the last day, and here we are. Your Honour, that's our protest. It has had the effect - a number of factors have contributed to that - it has had the effect that, leaving aside what Mr. Tieger said about the last word going to Mr. Krajisnik, which we suggest is more than fair, more than apt in the way that's contemplated, it's had an effect that on a very significant part of the case, effectively the Prosecution have had the last word. Your Honour, we hope and trust it won't matter in the end, but Your Honours now have the -- we've described it as daunting and it remains daunting. Your Honours have the daunting task of sifting the mountains of material, and Your Honours have the daunting task also of applying to that material the often complex, sometimes abstruse, but always significant jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Having said that, Your Honour, we on the Defence side are going to do what we understood what we were here to do today, and we are going to reply. And we're going to do it within that sort of time and we're going to give Your Honours our brief comments on the points that have been made which we understood was the nature of the exercise today, and then when we've done that, with one or two short codas, we will sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, may I ask you one thing? It is because you're using the same word "daunting" again. This morning I saw myself, together with one of my colleagues, trying to find out exactly what it means in our dictionary. Could you describe it in such a way, what you actually -- because we found a couple of meanings which -- all of them, we thought, is that really what Mr. Stewart had in mind? So, as non-native speakers, we'd like not to miss one word.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I suppose the answer is that it is exactly what I have in mind because I feel I know what the word means. But Your Honour's question nevertheless is perfectly fair. It's going to be an imperfect definition, then. What I have in mind anyway, Your Honour, is that it is -- it's a challenging, perhaps verging on the frightening - but I'm not suggesting Your Honours will be frightened, of course - but it is a challenging, could be to some people frightening task. It is a difficult, heavy task. If you're facing a very steep cliff on a mountain and you're going to have to climb it - perhaps it's Mr. Harmon that's going to have to climb it - it would be daunting. It might not be daunting to Mr. Harmon, I don't know, but it would be daunting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how I understood it, and that's what we do not find in the Oxford dictionary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. I didn't look there for it, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you but since we spent some time on it this morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My curiosity is going to be to see what the French word is later that comes through as the translation of "daunting." It will be interesting to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I'm going to do then is, exactly the way I've said, first of all just comment very briefly on the ten points, I think it was, that Mr. Gaynor went through in his submissions. Mr. Gaynor is going to be the focus of our attention this afternoon. The first of the ten issues he raised - and this was at page 56 of Tuesday's LiveNote transcript - I apologise, I don't know whether we've had the proper numbered version. I'm working from the LiveNote one here. At page 56, was 98(H)(ii). We really don't quarrel with the broad propositions as set out in Mr. Gaynor's submissions, and a lot of it does boil down, of course, to judicial common sense. But we -- again we give one particular illustration of the sort of problems that arise in this case. And it's not the only one; it is an illustration. At page 55 of the same transcript on Tuesday, Mr. Harmon said: "Finally, Your Honours, if you look at Defence Exhibit 211, it's a document from the Pale Executive Committee dated the 7th of July that is addressed personally to Biljana Plavsic and informs Mrs. Plavsic that Muslims started moving out forcefully and willfully at their own private -- it must be initiative -- and discretion --" and it goes on, and then Mr. Harmon's contention there was: "Mrs. Plavsic surely would have shared that information with Mr. Krajisnik." Well, that's what he invites as the conclusion. It's that document, 211, which has not been dealt with -- it's obviously been produced, but it's not been referred to in the case, except at the point when Mr. Krajisnik, in the course of his evidence, that document was presented. Even then he did not have the opportunity to expand upon those documents. And Mrs. Plavsic was not asked about that document at all when she gave evidence. That is, in a way, extraordinary, but it highlights where we are in relation to unput points and unput material. The conclusion just being that if something hasn't been put, hasn't been considered, then of course Your Honours must be extraordinarily cautious before drawing any adverse conclusion, any adverse inference at all towards Mr. Krajisnik. Otherwise, Your Honours, we've made quite full submissions on most of these points in our final brief. We don't add anything there. Mr. Gaynor did, under this point, at page 60 - this is page 60, line 15 - say, "In respect of assessing credibility, the Chamber had ample opportunity to observe the accused and to draw its own conclusions about the accused's credibility during the 40 days of his evidence. For these reasons, all the concerns underlying Rule 90(H)(ii) were addressed." That's a different point. Opportunity to assess credibility is a different point. It's part, of course, of the overall assessment of evidence. But this point under Rule 90 goes to the opportunity of dealing with such material and what inferences are then fair to draw. The third point Mr. Gaynor dealt with at page 61, line 6, the next point, I'm quoting him, is that "joint criminal enterprise liability can apply to a massive criminal campaign." That's his point. "The Defence appears to argue at paragraphs 107 and 130 to 134 of its brief that JCE liability cannot apply in a large-scale case. This issue has already been considered and dismissed." We don't say that, Your Honour. That's an extreme position we don't adopt. We do say that it's, in many ways, not apt to apply. We've covered this in our brief. The key point is that JCE is a mode of liability for committing particular crimes, and that nexus is the key, the nexus between the defendant and the crimes. And as long as that key point is focused on, then -- as long as that key point is focused on, then what we say in the Defence brief is correct and does not go as far as is suggested. The -- I had, I think, in going through, I'd inadvertently skipped over -- that was in fact the third point. I did inadvertently skip over the second point, which is at the foot of page 60, line 23. His second point, in fact, was the mens rea, the planning, ordering and instigating as set out in the Defence brief was incorrect, and he referred to the submissions in paragraphs 92 to 96 of the Defence brief, and suggested that because we had not specifically acknowledged and recognised what was said in the Kordic appeal judgement at 25 to 32 -- paragraphs 25 to 32, we had misstated the law. Your Honours, we simply observe that, on a proper reading of what we say in the Defence brief, there is no inconsistency. Your Honours will see very clearly what the proper legal test is to apply. The fourth point, at the bottom of page 61, 61, line 20, the application of JCE 3 liability has been sufficiently covered in the Defence brief. The fifth point, at the foot of page 62, that's line 24, JCE does not require an agreement between the accused and those physically carrying out the crimes, we have also really quite fully covered in the Defence brief. The sixth point is first referred to at page 65, but in fact then there's an interjection and it really starts at page 66. The sixth point is that the JCE liability does not require that the accused make a substantial contribution. Mr. Gaynor referred to the Defence brief, stating at paragraph 143 that for JCE liability to attach, the accused must have carried out acts that substantially assisted or significantly affected the furtherance of the goals of the enterprise, and draws attention to the fact that we did not refer there specifically to the Kvocka appeal judgement and to paragraph 97. Your Honours, it's necessary to read the whole of paragraph 97. I don't mean now. But it's of course necessary to read the whole judgement of the Appeals Chamber in Kvocka so far as it's applicable. But in particular, the whole of paragraph 97 needs careful reading. And we suggest that whatever the nuances of Kvocka, in the case where the Court was not satisfied that the accused's acts had either substantially assisted or significantly affected the furtherance of the goals of the enterprise, it would be necessary to be extremely cautious before entering into imposing criminal liability on the basis of the nuances of what we find in Kvocka. Paragraph 7, we do not wish to add anything -- I'm sorry, point 7. It's at page 66, line 13. The next point, Mr. Gaynor says, is also short. The Defence brief at paragraphs 152 to 154 makes submissions concerning aiding and abetting. We have nothing to add there to that, except to say that this is an area where a reading of the indictment wouldn't necessarily have enabled anybody to see very clearly what was being said on these particular points. And, no doubt, that was a difficulty facing the draftsman of the indictment at the time as well. On paragraph -- point 8, rather, which is at page 66, line 20, there's a submission in relation -- there's a reference to the Defence final brief at paragraphs 260, 266 to 270; a conviction for genocide under Article 7.3. In the Defence submission, the Prosecution must establish that the accused possess the requisite dolus specialis. The only support for this view is Stakic Rule 98 bis as the Defence brief appears to accept that there's a considerable quantity of jurisprudence against the Defence. Your Honours, again, that point is clearly seen, or the elaboration of that point is clearly seen from the briefs. We add nothing to what we have said in our written brief. The next point, point 9, page 67, line 11, Mr. Gaynor: "The next point concerns the expanded Presidency." Line 14 Mr. Gaynor says: " I simply wish to add that as a matter of law it is not in fact necessary to prove that the accused held any de jure authority to secure a conviction under Article 7.3." Your Honour, we don't say it is. That's not our submission. Our submission doesn't go that far. Mr. Gaynor continues: "A finding of de jure authority does establish a rebuttable presumption of effective control, but the controlling test for liability to attach is whether the accused in fact held effective control." But, Your Honours, we do persist, and it's in our final brief and it's covered, we do say, there was not de jure authority. All that means is the Court must then establish the correct jurisprudence, so it must apply the correct jurisprudence in relation to de facto authority, depending, of course, on the findings on the evidence. And Your Honours have our submissions that, on the facts and the evidence, that that is not established anyway. But we -- our submission on the de jure authority is not correctly represented in that passage of the Prosecution's submissions. And then on the tenth point, at page 67, line 23, in relation to intent to commit crimes in each indictment municipality, we have nothing to add. And, again, we stand on what we set out in our written final brief. Your Honour, then turning to the answers to the questions given today, question 1 -- and I'm just going to give the numbers, Your Honour, I'm not going to read out all the questions again. It's on the Trial Chamber's list. We have nothing to add. None of this means we agree with the Prosecution, Your Honour. That's obviously not the point. Question 2, we agree -- of course where we specifically say we agree, we do. We agree with what was said about the impermissible -- or impermissibly cumulative nature of 7.1 and 7.3 convictions. Not surprisingly, we do go along with that. Otherwise, we have nothing to add on that point. We have nothing to add on question 3 to our submissions already made. So far as question 4, JCE 2, is concerned, Your Honours have our submission that it does not aptly fit this case. But you also have our submissions, both in the final brief and yesterday, on the inter-relationship of JCE 1 and JCE 2. Question 5, the Mauzer point. Well, Your Honours dealt with that. It's really unnecessary for me to add anything there. So far as 6 is concerned, we don't easily see how that question has been fully answered by the Prosecution in any case. But we do make one particular comment there. Mr. Gaynor said, "There was no evidence that Karadzic did not know about the events in Bratunac prior to this meeting." That rather odd way of expressing the matter does just lead us possibly to one final reminder to everybody as to where the burden of proof in this case lies. Paragraph -- question 7, the answer on Crisis Staffs did, at least to some extent and very belatedly, clarify the Prosecution case. And that and 8, particularly question 8, the answer there was, well, it was a classic final brief question, really. This is probably the clearest example of what should have been in the final brief, or at the very least in the first round of oral submissions. But perhaps, in the end, none of it is terribly surprising and it's all part of the evaluation exercise, that daunting exercise, facing the Trial Chamber. And question 9 was at least answered on Tuesday. Your Honour, those are our submissions today. I'm going to end on a positive note, because I've finished the submissions. I would just like to add very briefly, because I did associate the Defence with some compliments and thanks issued by the Prosecution, I would like to take the opportunity of thanking my own team. I hope that Your Honours feel that that's appropriate, because some of them have been with me a long time. In fact, Mr. Jonovic has been with me a very long time. Sometimes he's full-time and sometimes he's part-time. But when he's full-time, he's really full-time, like all the members of the team. Mr. Rasiah is a recent member of the team, but full-time is a severe understatement as to his contribution to the case recently. And of course Mr. Josse is both the recipient of my enormous thanks for his part in the case. He came into the case in a way that required him not so much to just jump into the deep end, but then to swim under water for quite a long time before he was reasonably expected to surface. But he surfaced very quickly, and he's both the recipient of the thanks, and I also know that he's associated with me in giving the thanks to the rest of the team. And my thanks extend to all past and present members of the team. Their contributions can be very clearly seen on the record, the long record, of this case. In whatever hemisphere they currently find themselves in, the thanks extend to all of them. They are heartfelt. I have had enormous support. It seems that occasionally some of them have even enjoyed working on the team, which is always heartening to see. Mr. Krajisnik is going to have the last word, of course. I would just like to say in relation to Mr. Krajisnik, and perhaps if I may be permitted, slightly through Your Honours to Mr. Krajisnik: All clients and counsel have their ups and downs in a long case. I would just like to say that no counsel could have a more courteous and industrious client than Mr. Krajisnik, and I do wish to acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. I'd suggest that we now put a few questions, only a few questions, to the parties on some points, sometimes even minor points. But we'll then have a break, and then before the break I'll read and explain the Rule 84 bis to Mr. Krajisnik, which I think is appropriate under these circumstances, and then Mr. Krajisnik will have an opportunity make his statement after the break. And that would then conclude this trial. Perhaps a few -- one question for you, Mr. Stewart. The Prosecution has argued that Rule 90(H)(ii), confronting a witness or putting to a witness what your case is - would not apply and they have given some authorities for that position - would not apply if an accused testifies, if I understood you well, Mr. Gaynor. I haven't heard any position taken on this matter by the Defence. Would you agree with Mr. Gaynor, which of course leaves totally apart how Rule 90(H)(ii) was applied view of other witnesses, or do you disagree with him on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we completely disagree. We say it's simply wrong. That it just applies and there isn't such an exception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the material he -- I have not reviewed it yet, so therefore I was wondering whether you had an opportunity. He cited a few cases, I think a Canadian case and Australian case. Do they support or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the underlying principle is, after all, one of fairness. It may be that, in particular circumstances, the defendant or party himself - because some of those citations are civil cases - has been fully alerted to points in a way that other witnesses might not. But that's all it comes to, really. It's still -- the concept is a fair opportunity to deal with points and a fair exploration of evidential points so that one isn't left with material which is untested. If something -- it becomes one-sided, then. If something is put forward and then there hasn't been a fair opportunity given for it to be tested, explained, answered, that's essentially what the principle is. It's an illustration, if you like, or it's a subcategory of the essential fairness of the whole process; that there must be a fair opportunity to answer, there must be a fair opportunity to deal with points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There might be several elements in the Rule where I, perhaps, was more thinking about -- let me just have a look. Yes. I thought that part of the Rule was that a witness should not be uninformed that his testimony contradicts the Prosecution case so -- because if he would not be informed, he might not understand what kind of explanation would be needed. And I think part of your argument was, Mr. Gaynor, that if an accused testifies in his own case and has been present from the beginning in that case, has followed all the opening statements, has seen all the decisions, that under those circumstances, that the need to give this information to a witness is certainly less pressing than for a witness who comes into the case and may not have seen one single aspect of it and is totally unaware where the friction between his testimony and the case of the Prosecution, the case of that party, would be. I'm just putting it to you what I thought was the argument and how I understood that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as it goes, that's correct. As far as it goes. I think I acknowledged a few minutes ago that there may very well be, as a starting point, a difference between the position of the defendant -- not -- he is, in a sense, just a witness in the case, but for the sort of reasons Your Honour's just summarised. Of course the defendant will know and should know, in the progress of the case, what is against him. But the difficulty about applying that distinction to the present case is that that -- that difference is clearer and satisfactorily deals with the situation in a relatively simple case. Where you have a case of this complexity and this range of material, of course Mr. Krajisnik, and of course the Defence team, have known long before he came to give evidence or long -- well, pretty early, as all witnesses came to give evidence, what the case was against him in its essentials. But as soon as you get one layer below, into all the evidential matters that might be explored, you can't know then. You can't anticipate what all those points are. So if a point -- it comes back to the point, if something is then going to be relied upon -- we gave a tiny example, a tiny but telling example earlier this afternoon. That's what makes it so important to put the points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That certainly clarifies your position. Mr. Gaynor, I asked you earlier today a question on -- well, more or less asking what your understanding is of the words "talking to," which for me suggest a conversation. I'm afraid that I'm addressing the wrong person. I heard during the -- and I read in the final brief on the issue of knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik that -- let me just find it. It reads in paragraph 397, it says: "Mirko Krajisnik informed Krajisnik about the Ahatovici massacre," and then the reference is made to P292 and P239. When I read the transcript of that telephone conversation, I hear Mirko Krajisnik saying that the bus was attacked by Muslims and that they, perhaps mistakenly, thought that all those in the bus were Serbs. Now, if I read that text - I mean, you can say he gave false information or you could say the information was right - but to bluntly state "Mirko Krajisnik informed Krajisnik about the Ahatovici massacre," yes, at close reading of course it's correct, because Mirko Krajisnik, in that telephone conversation, informed about the massacre. But of course it is in the context of the knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik about reports and information, not about what Muslims had done but about what Serbs had done. I was a bit surprised by this way of using the material, and I'd like to give you an opportunity to explain what made you translate -- apart from being cut on the number of pages, what made you present it in this way and whether you would not agree that the Chamber would be -- could better look at the details by another presentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first of all, the mere fact that the Court brings this matter to our attention in this manner is sufficient indication to us that, as the Court said, there might be a preferable way of doing it. The reality of what's communicated here is, as the Court indicated, the Prosecution pointing the Court to the fact that Mr. Krajisnik was advised about the event. I do regret for -- that it wasn't clarified. I'm not going to make the excuse of space limitations, but that plays a role in all of this. We pointed the Court to the specific intercept, so obviously there was no intent to mislead in that respect. I would have welcomed the opportunity, for example, to point out the factors that make that telephone conversation significant, including the location of where it happened, the proximity of the location to both where Mr. Krajisnik lived and where Mr. Mirko Krajisnik lived, the general knowledge surrounding events at that time, the forces arrayed at that time. I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour, I don't want to add to the brief now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly what was on Mr. Stewart's mind. But you would say if you had an opportunity to give more details, then you would have given a bit more reasons why it was relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Only two things can happen in this case: Either, based on all the evidence in the case, the Court will make that connection, or the Court will look at it and say, Well, that's not sufficient support for the proposition. But surely there's no attempt to mislead by pointing the Court directly to that intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in your final brief, I read in paragraph 215: "Bosnian Serb Crisis Staffs were originally formed secret SDS party organs in accordance with Variant A and B." We have a few Crisis Staffs that were established before the 19th of December, 1992, and where it is -- where one could expect that if Crisis Staffs were formed considerably later than December 1992, that the Prosecution would say, Well, they were late, or they were delayed in doing what they had to do. But what about the Crisis Staffs that were formed before the 19th of December? Of course, you could say it's in accordance with. Would they have the same kind of tasks? How do you explain that they were formed in these earlier stages? What's, then, the causal relationship between the instructions and those Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first of all, I wish I could call to mind the particular Crisis Staffs to which the Court is referring. I do have one in particular in mind, but only vaguely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't have the names here, but I remember one very early and then another one, I think, in mid-October or something like that. I couldn't give you at this moment the -- I just have -- I think I have two in my mind. But yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think what's most important to bear in mind with respect to those is their continuing connection to the Bosnian Serb leadership. And if you follow the activities of those bodies, and although I can't point the Court to - apparently the Court can't either - to the specific ones, my clear recollection is that those Crisis Staffs did not operate on a path outside of that undertaken by the many, many, many Crisis Staffs established in response to Variant A and B, but in much the same way, and were established -- I don't want to focus on their establishment so much because I can't at the moment recall either the particular dates or the particular trigger. What I do know is that they, and especially after December 1991, acted in a manner consistent with all the other Crisis Staffs that were formed pursuant to Variant A and B and for the same purpose and under the direction of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Now, whether or not they were stocking horses or -- I do recall one, for example, that was formed in the wake of, to the best of my recollection, the state of emergency that Dr. Karadzic declared on October 18th. There was clearly a sense of events moving forward, as we know, after the October 14th and 15th joint Assembly session. So we had the October 15th political council meeting. Immediately thereafter, the October 18th Deputies' Club, the October 18th state of emergency by Dr. Karadzic, and a considerable amount of attention. You'll see many intercepts where Dr. Karadzic is talking about the steps he's going to take. And my recollection is at least one of those, if you'll pardon the term, "premature Crisis Staffs" was formed at that time, very much in response to the situation and in light of the understanding that the Bosnian Serb leadership intended to move things forward so that municipal authorities could be established. So our position would be they were established for essentially the same purpose and followed the same path and were equally beholden, certainly after December 1991 and well prior to that, to the same authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps later I'll find the names of the two and the dates of the early establishment. There's one other matter, but that's really a very tiny, unimportant matter. If I look at your footnote 360, that's P65, tab 94, pages 40 to 43, it is supposed to contain what Mr. Cizmovic stated on the 28th of February, 1992. I don't -- it's not necessary that you respond immediately, but since it's the last day in court, I would have otherwise asked you to find that out. I do not see Mr. Cizmovic speaking on those pages, if I'm right. Perhaps there will be a second --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course we'll check that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My recollection is that that was the subject of some discussion during the course of Mr. Krajisnik's cross-examination. So if it's not, we'll get back to you as soon as possible, of course. But that might be another way in which to check the particular reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Another matter, and I first now address the Defence, although the question will not be for the Defence. The Defence has raised the issue of whether aiding and abetting a JCE would be at all possible, and then you continue, the Defence says it is charged in the indictment. We have serious doubts whether that is possible at all. But if it's possible, then this and this and this would be required. Could you comment on to what extent, apart from whether you could aid and abet to a JCE or, I mean the JCE being not a crime always. I was taught that you have to -- aiding and abetting is aiding and abetting to a crime and not to some -- perhaps, Mr. Gaynor, you could perhaps clarify the issue. It's been specifically raised by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think in my submissions on Tuesday, I referred Your Honour to a specific finding, and that is the Kvocka appeal judgement at paragraph 91, which held that it is indeed inaccurate to refer to aiding and abetting a joint criminal enterprise. So that form of liability, it appears, has been recognised as non- -- not fully --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it still appears in the indictment, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say we adopt a non-existing -- and Defence has the opportunity to say, well, yes -- so we can ignore that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I know the Defence has made submissions for what are the elements of that form of liability. But given that the Appeals Chamber considers that it's not a safe route to proceed, our submission is that Your Honours should not proceed down that route. And the Defence submissions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to -- aiding and abetting to a crime that was committed by the JCE. Is that a possibility? Just start --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, aiding and abetting a participant in the JCE appears to be fully accepted. That's also what the Kvocka appeals judgement, I think, says. But joint criminal enterprise itself is a form of liability. Aiding and abetting are a form of liability. When two forms of liability are mixed together, the picture becomes unclear. I think that's the point that the Appeals Chamber was making. To say that there's certainly a possibility to aid and abet a participant or a number of participants or a category of participants who are JCE members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you agree that mixing up two forms of liability would always be confusing or would you adopt that as a general rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll just consult for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to -- perhaps -- if I instigate someone to commit an offence, Well, you could do this, and I instigate and encourage him very much to do it, and then at the very moment when he's about to commit the offence, I'll help him, giving him a tool or whatever, that would be instigating and aiding and abetting, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. I agree that it's a very factual-based analysis, that on a very simple crime, that a crime can consist of instigating partly and aiding and abetting partly and committing. And I think there's a good example in the Gacumbitsi appeals judgement where the accused was present at a massacre site, he ordered that a massacre take place, he participated in separating Tutsi from other people, and he encouraged those present to begin the killing process. So in that situation, different forms of liability in respect to the various stages do seem to reflect correctly his criminal responsibility. So as a general proposition, I think, Your Honours, the law does seem to recognise that Your Honours can find -- in analysing the criminal responsibility, you can make findings under different heads of Article 7.1. However, mixing forms of criminal responsibility under 7.1 with joint criminal enterprise does not appear to meet with strong approval in the case law so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart asked specific attention to paragraph 97 of the Kvocka case, a substantial contribution where, in that paragraph, even without reading it as a whole, it's stated that it depends on the circumstance and it might well be that sometimes it is -- there is a need to establish that there was a substantive contribution. Any comment on -- because you put it very briefly and say, That's not required. But at the same time, in paragraph 97, of course, we find that it may well be required under certain circumstances. So therefore the question is whether we are facing such circumstances in this case. It's not an answer to the problem to say, in general terms, because the Appeals Chamber says it depends very much on where you are in whether such a substantial contribution should be established. Now, apart from the general rule that it is not always necessary, is this a case where it should be established?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, our position is that the accused in this case made a very substantial contribution to the joint criminal enterprise. So the matter is really a technical one in this case. I think what the Appeals Chamber was saying at that paragraph was that, as a matter of law, it is not necessary to establish that the accused made a substantial contribution to the JCE; however, as a matter of assessing evidence, it is easier to find that the accused participated in the JCE if he made a substantial contribution. As we've made submissions, the participation of this accused in this JCE was very substantial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see. Yes, Mr. Tieger, perhaps to assist you, Bosanski Petrovac, 24th of October, 1991 -- by the way, I misspoke earlier when I referred to the 19th of December, 1992. I meant, of course, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's Bosanski Petrovac. Well, you dealt with matters that happened in October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the same may be true about Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that was established in response to the 18 October state of emergency, and then disbanded and then reformed upon the dissemination of Variant A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Bratunac was also another one. Yes, that's -- I had two on my mind. I think these are the only two that are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might offer one quick additional clarification of an issue we addressed before, the Ahatovici prisoners. Again, I'm only trying to focus on any concern that the reference was misleading. One of the factors was that it was addressed in Mr. Krajisnik's examination, and my recollection is that he acknowledged knowing that it was Muslim prisoners who were killed. I think he also explained how he was told, as in the intercept -- I think he was shown that particular intercept, in fact, and I believe that's at - let's see if I have the page number, Your Honour-

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you're saying now -- we'll have a look at it --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is that there may be more support for what we find on this item in your final brief, more than what at this moment you have in the footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. And it's slightly beyond that. Enough so that the reference was a snapshot of that and we thought would be understood in light of it actually being raised in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let me see. Yes, I think ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no further questions for the parties. Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I briefly introduce this, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because I think I should point this out on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik. The statement that he prepared some time ago, as I mentioned yesterday, was translated. I gave that to my learned friends for the Prosecution yesterday. They considered it; they made some remarks. I've discussed those with Mr. Krajisnik. He has made a few additional remarks pursuant to the submissions that the Prosecution made two days ago, and so the Prosecution are not aware of everything that Mr. Krajisnik is going to say and I have informed them of that fact this morning, after my visit to the Detention Unit. In addition to that, trying to smooth the matter as best we can, we have provided to all three translation booths the B/C/S original and the English translation of what Mr. Krajisnik is going to read. But as I have already stated, there are a few corrections that he's going to make that don't appear necessarily on those documents. And secondly, he's going to extemporise, to a limited extent, at one juncture in the address that he wishes to make to the Chamber. I emphasise, Your Honour, that I explained that to Mr. Tieger this morning after I had returned from the Detention Unit. Finally this: Simply for information, Mr. Tieger stated that Limaj was prevented from making an 84 bis statement because he had testified.
