I'm informed by someone who's been following these proceedings that though that is true, the reason Limaj was unable to make that statement was because he had made an opening statement pursuant to Rule 84 bis. I mention that for information only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that information. Mr. Josse, I take it that you're aware of what are sensitive issues for the Prosecution as far -- the portions that are added, did you identify anything you'd consider to be of such a sensitive character?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, and -- I did not. Could I also emphasise that my learned friends were most cooperative and reasonable about the matter. Some of the passages I was frankly a bit concerned about they had, so to speak, sanctioned in any event. Nonetheless, Mr. Krajisnik and I, jointly, have edited a reasonable amount of his original effort, partly in view of the time that the Chamber is going to allow him. Your Honour, the 84 bis statement will take Mr. Krajisnik at least three-quarters of an hour, perhaps nearer an hour. I am bound to submit on his behalf that it does appear the Chamber has the time, and to hurry him at the end of over 300 days of hearing would be most unfortunate, we'd submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees to proceed as suggested, Mr. Josse. We'll give an opportunity to you, Mr. Krajisnik, to make your statement after the break. However, before the break, although it may well be that you have discussed it already with counsel, I'd like to point out that Rule 84 bis says, and although it's usually not -- it was not adopted as introducing the last word, but that's the way we use it, but it's still a statement under Rule 84 bis. That means that we allow you to make a statement. That statement is still under control of the Trial Chamber, although we hope that the way in which it was prepared allows us to not intervene at any moment and just to listen to you rather than to interfere with your statement. It is an unsworn statement, which means that you don't take an oath for that. In many systems, an accused never takes an oath, and in those systems that is not considered to be an invitation not to tell the truth. But you'll not make any solemn declaration, and oath, of course, is not the right word in this Tribunal. You'll not be examined about it. No one will be in a position to put any questions to you about it. We'll just listen to you. At the same time, the Chamber, as the Rule says, shall decide on the probative value, if any, of the statement. That means that you should be fully aware that if you say something, that we could, during our deliberations, accept what you said and use that in whatever direction; against you, in favour of you. We'll have to consider what probative value it has. And when we're talking about probative value, you should be aware that it's not only that you admit something or that you say that something happened in December, but also if you say something which is very much consistent with the evidence we received, we might understand that as -- well, we see that you're consistent in your approach of the case. But it's also possible that if you come up with something, an explanation or something else, which would be difficult to understand in view of the evidence we have, we might also draw negative inferences out of that. It's your statement, and we'll decide on the probative value. It might well be that we say it has no probative value at all. But you should be fully aware of that. I already now announced that after the break, when you've made your statement, that that concludes the trial in this case. I'm not going to thank everybody. That doesn't mean that this Chamber doesn't share the feelings that were expressed already in respect to people in this courtroom, outside the courtroom, but I'm not going -- Mr. Krajisnik, your statement will be the last matter we'll hear. We'll then, after having heard your statement, we'll start our deliberations on the judgement, and the next thing you'll hear from us is then the judgement. So, therefore, if there's any matter which the parties would like to deal with before the end of this trial, then please raise it now. It's like in a marriage: If there's any objection, bring it now or be silent forever, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In the expectation that this is the last time I'll rise in this case, I just wanted to respond quickly to the Court's inquiry about the, I think, footnote 360.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. The reference to pages 40 to 43 were a reference to an older translation that was -- and the proper reference should be 29 to 31, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. So if there's nothing else, then we'll now have a break. We'll resume at 25 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber gives you the opportunity to make a statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, I should like to thank you for having it made possible for me to address you with my closing remarks, this being my last attempt at proving the truth. I am satisfied that I have done everything within my power, participating in the presentation of evidence, in assisting my Defence team, and in the preparation of documents, and I would have, indeed, regretted the fact had this last attempt been denied to me. Thank you, Your Honours, and I thank everybody for making it possible for me to make these closing remarks. As I was preparing my closing remarks to address this Trial Chamber, I was in a dilemma. I asked myself, What should I say as I summarise a job that my Defence has been doing over the last six and a half years? Not only was it a challenge for me because I undertook a task that I had never faced before but also because I was doing it in a matter which involved myself. In fact, I even had the feeling that I would have performed a similar task more successfully if I had been doing it on someone else's behalf. Also, I was additionally burdened by the fact that I had to deal with a portion of my own life and that I had to unplug my emotions lest I be accused of failing to maintain the required level of objectivity. Such were my thoughts before I composed this text and before I could say to myself unequivocally that I was a hundred per cent certain that the difficult decision to read from prepared remarks was the correct one. That is why I was perhaps at a certain point leaning towards not writing anything but speaking extemporaneously and saying what I felt and believed would be appropriate to articulate in these closing remarks. I nevertheless rejected the idea of addressing the Chamber extemporaneously, without the benefit of a written text. I decided to compose a final statement, not only because I wished in that way to express my respect for the Chamber and for everyone else who has been following these proceedings over the last two-and-a-half-year period but also for the sake of history, which is something I regard very highly. Therefore, for the sake of history and for my own fate as well, right at the outset, I wish to say the following to Your Honours: I address you as a man who believes in God and Divine justice. I believe in truth and its ultimate triumph. I believe in justice and truth because, were I to believe that injustice and untruth could prevail in the end, the world would lose its meaning for me. But I want the world and the people who share those values to survive, and I take this view because I consider that the truth can bother only those whose consciences are unclear and who've committed a crime or an injustice against someone else, and I am not to be found in that category of men. Having spent time in prison -- having spent, sorry, over six and a half years in prison in The Hague, as I have pointed out, on more than one occasion I have attempted to take stock of everything that I had done. And I invariably reached the same conclusion; that throughout my life I had acted consistently. I never consciously aligned with those who acted unjustly and inhumanely. If something resembling that ever did occur, it was without my knowledge or approval. I assure you that I would champion the truth, even if I had to pay a dear price for it and regardless of how dear the cost of that to me. I say this because it is my sincere belief because there is no statute of limitations for a crime. I do not mean that in the legal sense of the statute of limitations. I say that as a man who believes in God's statutes, according to which a crime might conceivably evade terrestrial justice but not God's, and his ultimate punishment which is generally much stricter and longer lasting than that of any earthly tribunal. If I were guilty but a Court acquitted me, I would be afraid that the punishment that should have been meted out to me would devolve upon my children. For all those reasons, Your Honours, although I fully appreciate that the key to my fate is in your hands, I will not, my respect for you notwithstanding, plead with you for mercy but will exhort you to rather decide according to the dictate of your conscience and with due regard only for the evidence that had been put before. I say this fully aware of the danger that it poses, because my Defence team did not put before this Chamber even a minimum quota of arguments to demonstrate my innocence and to convey my version of the truth, although all that was available to the Defence team from the very start of these proceedings. May I remind you: That is the consequence of the anomalies that have been plaguing my defence throughout these proceedings, something to which I had drawn attention repeatedly. Notwithstanding that, I address you with an appeal that you bring your judgement based on the evidence that has been heard, because my truth - as you have yourself reminded me on various occasions - was heard by a panel of experienced professional Judges and not by a jury, although I have nothing against a jury in principle. I believe that you have heard and seen sufficient evidence during the trial to enable you to come to a decision based on truth and justice. I say this because I am persuaded of it also by the position you've taken in the final stages of the trial when you decided that you did not need any additional witnesses or evidence from us. I gained the impression that you had already made your decision, or that you had reached a firm view. And I even go as for as to assume that final statements may be required more as a procedural formality than as an additional argument on behalf of the Defence. When I say that I am convinced that you have already reached your decision, I want to be frank and sincere to the very end: I'm convinced that your decision is a just one, and that you have arrived at the view that the indictment against me is entirely baseless. Prior to expounding the reasons why I claim that I am not guilty, I should like briefly to touch upon the final -- the closing arguments of the Prosecutor. Actually, I have written an entire reply to the Prosecutor's claims and submissions, but due to the briefness of time, I'm just going to enumerate a couple of these reasons. I've divided them into two groups; one is of a general and the other group are those of a specific nature. First of all, I should like to say that as I was listening to the closing arguments of the Prosecutor, I have to say that I was really -- I really was stressed out. I really was experiencing the kind of stress that I had experienced when I was arrested and brought here in my pyjamas. Unfortunately, I had many stresses in my life - when I lost my wife, when I lost my father, and on other occasions - but even though I was aware of the contents of the indictment, this is something I would not want no person in the world to experience. Therefore, Your Honours, with full esteem for the OTP and the Trial Chamber, I'm sure that you will bring your decision on the basis of the truth and not on the basis of assumptions, because it is true, as the OTP says, that terrible crimes have happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I'm saying this also on account of something else. Please bear with me. I'm very reluctant to say this: The Serbian people have a negative -- harbour a negative attitude towards the Tribunal at The Hague because they consider it to be putting only Serbs on trial. And I have put in so much effort to prove that this Tribunal is in fact the only venue where I can indeed prove my innocence. Having been charged so heavily under its indictment, this is where I have my opportunity to prove that the Speaker of the Assembly, the president of the Assembly, could not have commanded the army and have been in a position to command those people. So this is something which I appreciate, this opportunity. I should like to remind you, Your Honours, had I been guilty in the eyes of the Muslims and the Croats, they wouldn't have wanted me to be the first man in the Presidency, in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't want to go through the entire Dayton Accords procedure. They could have said that they didn't want me to be a member of the Presidency, of the Presidency in 1996. So had it been my intention, in other words, to destroy the Croats and the Muslims - I'm talking about just the Croats now - would our politicians have allowed that to happen? Would they have let the Muslims and Croats cross over to our territory, even bearing arms, through our territory to their own territory? Would we have allowed their treatment in our hospitals? We wanted good relations with the Muslims. We did everything in order for that to indeed materialise. We wanted to have good relations, because without the agreement of all the three peoples in Bosnia, nothing can function there. They said Mr. Krajisnik was able for that position, he is clever, and they spoke in commendable terms about me. If I were clever, gentlemen, I would not be here, I would not be facing this Tribunal. If I were clever, I would have learned how to avoid having to come here. I cannot understand, I fail to comprehend, after this entire trial, what is it that Momcilo Krajisnik could have done? I fail to comprehend this legal logic. And finally, we had 250 statements by different witnesses. We also had expert witnesses taking the stand, and you saw how many witnesses we were able to call and bring. Of course, a much better picture would have been painted if a larger number of people with credibility could have been called to either corroborate or disprove some of the claims made here. I have been accused of wanting devastation in Bosnia-Herzegovina by force. First of all, I should like to remind you that we had the Cutileiro plan first and foremost, and that on the basis of it we made our entities. It was a voluntary exercise. It was in place by March. By the 22nd of April, I went to see Alija Izetbegovic, the late Alija Izetbegovic, to the Assembly, so that we could reach an agreement. After that, on the 22nd of April, if you remember, Karadzic made this platform which we adopted at this sort of consultative meeting, and it said specifically negotiations, negotiations until we have a solution. On the 12th of May, we proposed to the European Community to conduct negotiations and never to stop those negotiations. Even if there is war, we should negotiate until a solution is achieved. Prior to the war, did we not have a session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska when Karadzic was asked what were our plans? We said we had no plans. If it should come to war, you will see what our plans are. Peace is what we uphold as our greatest value, and we are championing and fighting for peace. To a question by deputies, what are we to do? He said, when you go to your homes, create your Crisis Staffs. I just want to underline that we did not want to solve things by military might. But once war does arrive, you have no option but to actually accommodate your needs to that exigency because people are fighting. I should like to remind you that prior to the 12th of May we were in Geneva negotiating with the other two national communities in order to reach a solution. After that, we went to Grac to talk to the Croats to see what was disputable, what was controversial, also with the desire to arrive at a political solution. I was also accused that I said that the Muslims wanted an Islamic state. If you look at my statement, I said some of the representatives of the Muslim negotiating team called for an Islamic state. And as proof of that, I said that in Muhamed Filipovic's book, at page 57 and 58, it's clearly seen that Mr. Kouacevic [phoen], a professor, made an analysis, a study, and he justifies in it how an Islamic state -- the first one in the Balkans after the Ottoman Empire could be created. I just mention what some people were -- [B/C/S on English channel] -- Izetbegovic's team who were in favour of the creation of such an Islamic state. So this was probably a slip of the tongue that was referred to. Thank you. I apologise. It was horribly a slip of a tongue. It was said Glogova. Glogova allegedly happened at the instructions of the republic authorities, as represented by Goran Zekic. Please look at Deronjic's testimony. He said when Goran Zekic got killed, that same evening he started the Glogova action in retaliation. Maybe it was a slip of the tongue, but Goran Zekic could never have done anything about that. I'm also accused of having had the power to have some people released from prison. You gave two examples; Mr. Stanic from Ilijas and Mr. Karahmetovic where it was actually Mr. Mandic who arranged his release. Please, Mr. Stanic was a friend of mine from before. And I called the chief and asked him, Could you please let my Croat friend -- I called Trifko Radic. I called Mandic equally about the other man, Karahmetovic. I told him Karahmetovic is someone I used to play football with when I was a child. Those were a couple of cases, but there were many more in my life. In fact, I helped whenever I could help. Whenever I could ask for a favour on anybody's behalf, I did. About that girl that you remember, I have a girl of my own; of course I did it. I would have done, and I did, everything whenever I was able to. I'm sure you would have done the same if it were your colleague. It is claimed here that Muslims left Pale and that they were forced to leave. But, please, let me remind you Mrs. Plavsic was a commissioner at Pale precisely when it was happening, and when you asked her here, she said she didn't know a thing for the duration of that entire period when that was going on. I know it's hard to prove things here, but you should have asked her. Another charge that's leveled against me is that on the 11th of August, in Banja Luka, there was a proposal to include in the agenda the issue of prisoners, and allegedly I didn't allow it. Please, Your Honour, look at just one page in that transcript of that session. You will see that what I actually said is, We have another session tomorrow. Let the government prepare the background material and then we'll include it in the agenda. The government didn't prepare the background material, and without the background material, we were not able to discuss such an important matter. And the government failed to do that because ten days later they had a planned meeting in Banja Luka for which they had to make a report. The Prosecution also says that I knew about the arming of people. It was a long time ago. Let me just tell you, remind you in fact, that my own place, my birthplace, Zabrdze, did not have any weapons. And if I were to arm anybody, I would have armed them first to enable them to defend themselves. That's what a witness explained here, how they actually got the weapons. Dusan Kozic, and the distribution of weapons. I didn't find the words to explain it at the time. I didn't have time, in fact, to explain it. Please find that report. It doesn't have a stamp, it doesn't have an indicated addressee, it doesn't follow the procedural format. Please don't look at the English. In the way it was written in Serbian, it could never have been sent to anyone except as a working draft. I keep thinking about it, to this day, and I know now that I could never have received that report. Just another word about Davidovic. Davidovic said that he had seen a document to the effect that I ordered the ethnic cleansing of Bijeljina. I gave you two documents, and please look at them. He said he had given that document to Jerkovic. The document that I did indeed give speaks about when Jerkovic started to deal with changes. That was in '92. And I received another document whereby he was authorised by an MP, Milan Tesic, who was a commissioner for the government. Quite simply, I didn't find my way around at that moment. Another thing that was stated here was that Krajisnik was able to find out from Mrs. Plavsic, from Karadzic, from Koljevic, from Djeric, and then they say he was able to walk around Bosnia and Herzegovina and to get his own information. It's difficult for me to say this: From April until the end of August, I had a wife who was ill and three children I had to care for. I had my full-time job in the Assembly, and I was conducting negotiations at Pale. After the 3rd of August, I had three children to take care of on my own, and I couldn't simply go travelling around Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mrs. Plavsic says that I was able to see about the crimes myself. Nobody, nobody ever reported any crimes to me. They would have never done that. They would have come to me to brag about something or maybe ask me for a favour. If somebody had accused me of doing that, in fact of not travelling relative to a period two years later, then there would be some sense in it. Now, as for the extended Presidency, I will tell you literally in bullet points what was stated here, just to remind you. On the 25th of July, 1992, if you remember, when we set out to the London conference, there was this statement made by Karadzic that he was being accompanied by member of the Presidency Koljevic and Speaker of the Assembly Krajisnik. That same day there was another War Presidency meeting, and that's when the members of the Presidency took their oaths. Not before that. You have the record of that meeting. It's all written there. All those sessions and all those records, I'm not sure I saw them all at the time. Maybe I did, maybe I didn't. But Mrs. Plavsic said she hadn't seen a single one. All of those meetings were said to be held in the state of immediate danger of war. None of them was called a meeting held in a state of war. We had a witness here who spoke about those records. If you look at his testimony, you will understand why things were organised that way. Bogdan Subotic, Dragan Kapetan, Rajko Kasagic are among the witnesses who denied the existence of the extended Presidency. You have also Gojko Djogo. His evidence was not admitted. Milan Trbojevic is another one. And let me remind you, he said we considered that the extended Presidency was the three-member Presidency, and that Karadzic was on it. You will see that if you look at his testimony. Slobodanka Hrvancanin denied the existence of that Presidency as well. Momcilo Micic did too. There was no state of war at the time, and the record of that Presidency session of the 30th of November says exactly that the extended Presidency cannot be introduced, whereas in the Prosecution's version, somehow by mistake, it says "cannot be maintained." In fact, it should read "it cannot be introduced because of the state of war." If I had been that important as they claimed after the constitutional changes, I would have become president of the republic. Instead, I remained president of the Assembly and there were another two people included in the Presidency instead of me. Let me remind you of the constitutional law envisaging the establishment of the extended Presidency in a state of war. You have seen that, on the 30th of May, the government adopted that, gave it to Karadzic for his signature, and it was not discussed at the Presidency session on the 30th of May. There was just that decision about municipal Presidencies. It was scheduled for promulgation on the 1st of July, and the date of that decision is the 2nd of July. I looked at that decision made by the Muslim authorities. They made an official decision which reads: "Hereby we establish the extended Presidency in a state of war," et cetera, et cetera. On our side, that decision was never actually adopted and promulgated. Only on the municipal level was it done. There was only the decision about commissions adopted, not the decision on the extended Presidency. You have seen a relevant letter, that session of the Presidency of the 26th of October, 1992. At that session, on the record of that session, it says: "Momcilo Krajisnik, member," whereas the letter I wrote on that day to the Main Staff reads: "Momcilo Krajisnik, President of the Assembly," and signed by Momcilo Krajisnik with a stamp of the Assembly. If I had been member of that Presidency, I would have signed myself as such at least to the letter -- in the letter to the Main Staff. Another reference is made to the 1st of September, 1992. If you look at it, there are two sessions on the 1st of September. One of them includes a point of the agenda: "Find offices for the Assembly and the Presidency." Those were two separate bodies. There were several conclusions that state the government needs to consult with the president of the Assembly and with the Presidency. And in every record, every transcript, you will see that everybody understood clearly that those were two different bodies. Yes, we did -- we were based in one and the same building, but then we moved to different places. There is not a single order, decision, not a single paper that I signed as a member of the Presidency, and I think it is -- it has not been proved and it has not been substantiated in any way. At the end of the day I would have been aware of being a member of the Presidency and I would have been proud of it. Why not? It's a much higher post than president of the Assembly. Now, if you ask me on what I base this stand of mine that I'm not guilty, let me remind you why I believe that all parts of the indictment have proven to be baseless. First of all, although that in and of itself cannot be regarded as a criminal activity, it was demonstrated that I was not a leading member of the SDS. I base this assertion on the fact that, although I was an SDS member and also a member of the main board and of the personnel commission during the period covered by the indictment, that is not sufficient to make the finding that the person was a leading member of a political party, in particular because it is now clear that the main board of the Serbian Democratic Party, during the second half of 1991 up until April of 1992, when the armed conflicts broke out, was convened at most three times. During 1992 there was not a single meeting, nor was the SDS even functioning as a political party. Also, the personnel commission of the SDS did not hold a single session, nor did it make a single personnel decision. The personnel policy was the province of the executive board of the SDS, of which I was not a member and not a single session of which I attended. Several witnesses confirmed that the party and state functions were separate within the SDS. As an obvious example of that, the fact was adduced that Dr. Karadzic, as president of the party, did not stand for member of the BiH Presidency in the 1990 elections, whereas Alija Izetbegovic and Kljuic and Pejanovic and Krsmanovic, they were all candidates for the BH Presidency. So he was not a candidate for the -- for a member of the Presidency in the 1990 elections, as well as the fact that ministerial nominees for cabinet and other positions in BH were not party people. Just to remind you, with the exception of two Serb ministers who were SDS members, the rest of them were not members of parties but they were in authority; they were in power. There was a division between party and state functions, in other words. I was appointed member of the main board of the SDS in mid 1991, but that did not mean that I had become a party functionary. I was appointed in response to the party's political needs because of the renown in which I was held as president of the BiH National Assembly and not with a view to my being elected to a party position which would make an important and influential SDS member. Secondly, I was not a member of any executive body wherein I also include membership in the Presidency of the Republic of Serbia. Now I'm going to skip over this paragraph and continue with the next one. It is correct that I did attend those meetings, which were called Presidency meetings, just as members of the Presidency and cabinet members attended sessions of the National Assembly. But it was quite clear that they were attending them as guests, with a right to participate in the debate but without a right to any decision-making. Now, that is how I attended these consultative meetings. And the fact that an expanded Presidency, pursuant to the June 2nd, 1992, constitutional law was not formed was confirmed by three -- by key witnesses. These meetings were held involving leading political figures of the Republika Srpska, most often including numerous attendees, but those were consultative meetings, not meetings of a body. I say that those were not meetings of the body, although, since those meetings were attended by Presidency members, the three of them, such meetings would also be dubbed Presidency meetings. But although such meetings may have been held in conditions of an immediate threat of war, they cannot be related to the extended Presidency provided for by the constitutional law implementing the constitution of June 2nd, 1992, which dealt with the formation of an expanded Presidency. The fact which was established beyond doubt is that I never issued a single order or made a decision purporting to act as a member of an expanded Presidency, while Presidency members, as is only normal, were doing that. If the contrary were the case, at least one single document would have surfaced indicating that I did have the authority to punish perpetrators, to order an investigation, or to take any other measures to prevent the commission of criminal acts. It was determined beyond doubt that I was neither authorised to punish anyone nor did I have command over the army and the police, which was confirmed by all the witnesses unreservedly. And it is Mr. Subotic Bogdan, Mladen Kapetina, who were the minister of defence. It is these testimonies which are very important. Also, I did not have any information about the work of the government and its ministries, namely, I was not present at any government session after it was constituted on the 12th of May, 1992, and it was also determined that I did not have the right to influence the decisions of municipal organs. If you remember Mr. Tupajic's testimony, when you asked him, Could Krajisnik replace you? he answered, It was only the Municipal Assembly that had appointed me that could have replaced me. All this means that it cannot be concluded that I failed to take all measures to punish crimes or prevent them from being committed. And I can add to this: That on account of the poor functioning of telephone and other communication links during most of the time period covered by the indictment, I was not, nor was it possible for me to be, informed about conditions in the field of any crimes that may have been committed. They say -- you say I could have been informed by the deputies, but, gentlemen, we had the Banja Luka session of the Assembly on the 12th of May. It was only on the 25th of July that we had the second session of the Assembly, and we only spent a day there and then departed for the London conference. The 1st session, then, was on the 11th of August when we could again take up the issue, but we already had given the government instructions -- the government had already been given instructions to investigate crimes on the territory of Republika Srpska. So it is quite obvious in which period of time I could have had an opportunity to have any dealings with any deputies. Expanding on the above, I can also add that each and every meeting which I attended, and where the slightest doubt was expressed that somewhere crimes may have been committed, concrete steps were taken to check the facts and to punish possible perpetrators. Third, the six strategic goals and the instruction and organising organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina under exceptional circumstances, also known as the A and B Variants, it was demonstrated that these were not plans whatsoever, at least this is what our think, for a power takeover in regions that Serbs consider to be their national and ethnic territory. Beyond any doubt it was demonstrated that the six strategic goals were not adopted at the meeting -- at the session of the National Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina on May 12th, 1992. Only as part of a memorandum, as a piece of information. So it was not a decision in the Assembly decision sense of the word. Otherwise, the A Variant document was not implemented anywhere in Republika Srpska. Not in a single place. If you remember, in some of the municipalities which were referred to by the OTP, it was circulated, it was distributed, but it was not carried out consistently in practice. The six strategic goals were a political platform, and I know that. I participated in the preparations for the negotiations, and we knew what it was that we wanted to achieve with the negotiations and what we wanted to achieve with the international community. And we never were planning war or preparing for war. It is not true, therefore, that we had war objectives. This might have been distributed if found in the field. It might have been distributed by someone, but I really wasn't aware of that. It wasn't certainly the Assembly. Whether it was the party, I have no way of knowing. But we had no influence on that whatsoever, nor on the putting into practice of their conclusions. I have stated here why the six strategic goals were a political objective. I emphasised by mistake that Karadzic said at the time, at this 12th of May session, it was actually I myself who had said it, on page 37. The ERN number is 02149476, and I said, precisely talking about the corridors: "In our negotiations being conducted with the Croat national community, we stated that we would rearrange territories." Here? We never referred to the corridor. And you may see that if anyone has read it." This quote, which I referenced to the appropriate page of the minutes reflects clearly our intention to achieve the strategic goals by political means. Specifically, in relation to this second goal, we were seeking an agreement with the Croat national community, which was a majority population in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We had certain territories there; they had certain territories there. So by exchanging territories, we would also include the territory around Kupres. And on account of that, we held the Grac meeting. All attempts at showing that we wanted to achieve our strategic objective by wars have been clearly proven to be wrong. At that same session, we also adopt an appeal to the European Community that we urge a continuation of the conference until a political solution was found, and to prevent the possible continuation of an armed conflict. Let me remind you, gentlemen, this was on the 12th of May. On the 13th of May, there was a telephone conversation between Mr. Mladic and Unkovic. Mr. Mladic says we have to respect the truce which was agreed. On the same date, Madam Plavsic was talking to Mico Stanisic and telling him the bombing has to stop because we have to abide by the armistice, by the truce. I apologise. Thank you. On the 13th of May, we were, let me add, in Banja Luka, at a celebration of the MUP day. On the 14th of May - you have it in Mr. Zimmerman's book - Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic were at a meeting with him and I was in Belgrade. And when I was told here, You were aware of the bombing of Sarajevo, of the shelling of Sarajevo on the 14th of May, no, I wasn't aware. I wasn't there. I was at Pale. I should like to say why these strategic goals were a political platform. On the 12th of May, when we were proposing the negotiations pending a solution, not a single strategic objective had been actually achieved. If we had waged war for that, we would have said, Let us wait for a couple of months and then we will continue with the negotiations. But at that point we said quite clearly we cease all activities at this point; we want negotiations. There was a very strongly adduced thesis here that I was a powerful man. If we analyse some of the evidence placed before this Chamber, we may conclude that this allegation of the Prosecutor was not confirmed. In the majority of these instances, this is a question of misinterpreting some of my personality traits, which is far removed from the sort of power which could have had, as its consequence, the commission of crimes. Furthermore, the imputation to me of personal power is contrary to logic because, for that to be the case, at least one of two conditions would have to -- would have had to be met: Either I must have been invested with legal authority from which such power is derived, or I had usurped the power which was not properly and legally mine. All pertinent legislation clearly demonstrates that I could not have had the requisite legal authority and consequently I lacked the decision-making power. So what remains, then, is only the possibility that I had usurped someone else's authorities. In that event I should have confirmed that in my de facto conduct. And the fact that this never occurred, not in a single instance, was demonstrated by the evidence presented in this trial. My renown and popularity, which some people have called that - and I'm sure they exaggerate it - is something which I acquired as an official of Bosnia and Herzegovina, discharging the duty of president of the National Assembly and not as a functionary of the Republika Srpska. This shows that this is -- what is the issue here is my political prestige built up as a result of my work in the first multi-party Assembly, and that prestige, rooted in the political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in a Bosnia-Herzegovina where we had to deal with the fateful question for the destiny of the people in Bosnia -- of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was only later augmented in my capacity as president of the RS Assembly. I know, and I'm quite sure that God certainly knows that neither was I not vested with power as part of the public function that I performed nor did I expropriate that power from someone else, thus abusing my position within the political leadership of the Republika Srpska. To demonstrate to you that the thesis of my alleged power is completely unfounded, I will remind the Chamber of the evidence of some of the witnesses who testified on this topic. Initially, while under direct examination, following the deductive method, they attempted to portray my power, they were hard put to exemplify their allegation for the period covered by indictment about my alleged power. It appears tragicomical, but in fact this category of witnesses in fact have described my position in the most graphic way. But what they were describing was not my power but rather something fundamentally different, so far removed from power that it is difficult to comprehend the reason for their confusion. May I remind you, Your Honours, one set of witnesses said that I was known as a man who is faithful to his commitments, who keeps his word, and one, if he were to give a promise, would keep it. For all those reasons I was quite powerful in their eyes. Then others explained, trying to make sense of my power, by stressing the fact that I worked a lot and diligently, performing a variety of tasks, and that I was seeing a great many of people soliciting favours from me. They would comment that they considered me powerful because people would not be coming to me with their concerns unless I had the power to attend to them. So they drew the conclusion that if someone responds to such solicitation, he can be presumed to have the power to do so. And therefore they drew the conclusion also that I was powerful, although, as they themselves stated, they had no knowledge of the substance of my conversations with those parties or what the nature of the expectations from me might have been. They did not, in fact, know that the way in which I lent assistance to those parties was by channeling them to officials who were in a position to help them, and by giving them advice on how to resolve their problems. I may have interceded on their behalf by soliciting assistance from those who did, in fact, have the power to be of real help. So there was this woman with her flat and a problem, and I really could not turn her down. This was referred to by a protected witness. That was one of such cases. The third set of witnesses pointed out what they felt was the most important source of my power, and they revealed to the Chamber that I was powerful because I was performing successfully my duty as president of the National Assembly, thus gaining the support of a broad section of the public; not just of Serbia but also of other ethnicities. Actually, this group of witnesses would add to the above the fact that I took part in the negotiating process with the two other ethnic communities aimed at a political solution to the BiH crisis which helped me to achieve enormous prominence and popularity which they in turn converted into de facto power. They pointed to my participation in the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina as my most important function, one that, according to them, did not properly belong to me but from which I derived the bulk of my power. However, in saying that, they had turned things on their head and spoke quite inaccurately. They had forgotten or they deliberately glossed over the fact that the Serbian BH deputies, in the founding session of the Serb Assembly, on October 24, 1991, designated me, together with another five candidates - with Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Buha and Mr. Maksimovic - to represent the Serbian national community, ethnic community, in the negotiations with the Muslims and the Croats and their ethnic communities. They also failed to mention that it was precisely in response to their insistence "to have the delegation revitalised" that I proposed to the Assembly on at least two occasions - March 11, 1992, and July 25th, 1992 - to select someone else for the negotiations instead of me, and I suggested indirectly that some of them be appointed to the negotiating team, something that the deputies rejected. They glossed over the fact that the deputies did not wish to change the composition of the delegation precisely because they understood the point about "revitalising" the negotiating team as a reflection of the unsound personal ambitions of those who were making it and of their desire to take on a task surpassing their abilities. Had I not been indicted, I never would have discovered that someone could have regarded me as powerful because of my participation on a team which was working on issues of critical significance for the Serbian people. I therefore must now view that accusation as the result of the immaturity of certain individuals and of their personal jealousy, and not as proof of my power. This conviction of mine has been corroborated by some of the highest level political figures of the Republika Srpska who have given evidence before this Court. I believe the Chamber has reached that same conclusion after having listened to their testimony. Related to the above charges is the entirely baseless and untruthful testimony of witnesses Biljana Plavsic, invited by the Chamber, and Milorad Davidovic, on behalf of the Prosecution, concerning my alleged participation in criminal activities during the BiH conflict. Mrs. Plavsic in particular shockingly testified about arms dealings with the Muslim side in which I supposedly took part, and her allegation that she reported to the RS Assembly concerning this issue. Mrs. Plavsic levelled some grave charges against me, stating that in response to her question: "Must we sell weapons to the Muslim side?" She heard, in my presence, Mr. Karadzic's response that it was necessary. Further, she stated that my home in Zabrdze served as a weapons arsenal for that commerce, although it is precisely on the dividing line. It was close to the front line. The house, which was later devastated, where my father was killed, which was later targeted by my own neighbours. In response to that statement, it was my intention to put to her several questions which would have made it manifest that she was not speaking the truth. As I was denied the opportunity to cross-examine her on these matters, and since I was certain that neither this or any similar issue was ever on the Assembly's agenda, I decided to further review my recollections. I was puzzled by the following question: Was she deliberately misstating things in order to harm me, or has she, under the weight of her age, allowed malice to influence her perception of the facts? Unfortunately, the upshot of this little investigation of mine was the conclusion that her misstatement, rather than being a misperception of the facts, was more likely a deliberate attempt to drag my name through the mud. Unfortunately, it turns out that on this point Mrs. Plavsic has deliberately given false evidence. Many witnesses ascribed my close relationship with Radovan Karadzic as one of the sources of my power. This claim is made precisely by those who were nominated by Mr. Karadzic for high posts in the state and in the SDS. Mrs. Plavsic is a prime example, although there were many other witnesses to that. Mr. Djeric and Mrs. Plavsic were nominated by Mr. Karadzic to the highest posts, initially in Bosnia-Herzegovina and later in Republika Srpska. Mr. Karadzic nominated Mrs. Plavsic, not me, as member of the BH Presidency on behalf of the SDS, while Mr. Djeric was nominated first as minister of the BH cabinet and later first Prime Minister of the government of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When the two of them, as well as others, were being nominated in 1990 to high positions in the Bosnian government, I was bypassed. I was not nominated to any high post although I knew Mr. Radovan Karadzic. In contrast to them, I was nominated by the municipal committee of the SDS for Novi Grad as the reserve candidate for deputy on the regional Sarajevo ticket, which included candidates for more than 10 municipalities. Mr. Karadzic's representatives placed my name sixth, that is to say last on the ticket, and I was elected deputy only after a recount of the vote. When I eventually passed as the candidate, I was not nominated to be president of the Assembly. It was Mr. Trbojevic instead. And when he was rejected, not because he was not good enough but because the problem of regional quotas was a problem to the other MPs, I was appointed to that position. Your Honours, let me remind you when the constitution was changed in December 1991. If I was that important, why wasn't I nominated to be president of the republic? Why Mrs. Plavsic? Let me remind you the time after the war, after the Dayton Accord, when Karadzic abdicated from his post. He did not give it to me, neither as president of the state or as president of the party. Mr. Buha was elected president of the party and Mrs. Plavsic, head of state. At the time of the elections, nobody wanted to be member of the Presidency. Mrs. Plavsic became head of state; Mr. Buha, president of the party; and I, at the time, since they wanted me very much to become a member of the Presidency, I did. I agreed to membership in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since I see that time is pressing, I won't be able to read all of this. The Prosecution charged that the Serb side established parallel institutions with a view to destroying Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let me remind you of one session of the Assembly. In fact, I want to say that we only made reactive moves in reaction to the conduct of the Muslim side. The late Izetbegovic, in January 1991, came out then with his platform and reneged on his agreement for Bosnia to remain a part of Yugoslavia. They opted for independence. In April, the Serb side raised the issue of regionalisation as a political response, and regionalisation was a completely legal, constitutional option, as it used to be before the war. When even that failed, before the war, we issued that recommendation to suspend regionalisation, because it was already gaining a political dimension. Instead, we wanted to talk about the declaration. When those debates failed, negotiations started on the historical agreement between Muslims and Croats; Serbs, Muslims and Croats, in fact. However, the Muslims withdrew their approval later from that agreement. In September, Izetbegovic himself proposed a certain conclusion to the Assembly, and that was accepted; that nobody should impose any solutions upon anyone else; that instead we would negotiate, forever if it takes forever; that anything is better than waging war. And after that, in October, the Muslims again came up with a new document, the memorandum, to replace the declaration, with the same goals. On the 25th of January, we had that debate on the referendum. All it took was to make a decision to regionalise Bosnia-Herzegovina, and all of us would then take part in a referendum. The agreement was there. Mr. Cengic, President of the SDA, was there and the president -- the prime minister also. And they both agreed that yes, the government would prepare a regionalisation. We agreed. Only 10 minutes later, Izetbegovic again said their approval and said, No, we're going forward with the referendum. When Mr. Cutileiro came, we were so glad that we had reached an agreement. On the 20th of March already, the Muslim side, just before going to Brussels, the Muslim side comes up and says, We were just gaining time. We don't want a transformation of Bosnia-Herzegovina; we want something else. We will invite the opposition and all the patriotic forces. We want Bosnia to remain as it is. I was not working for a division of Bosnia, ever. I was always committed for Bosnia to remain a part of Yugoslavia, just as the entire Serbian side did. But when that failed, when we didn't get the other side to agree, we agreed to Bosnia-Herzegovina instead. And we said, Okay, let's transform it. Let us achieve some sort of autonomy within Bosnia. Your Honours, when we were proposing various options to the Muslim and Croatian side for Bosnia to be a perfectly autonomous state within Yugoslavia, in a very loose fashion, with only a couple of policies and institutions in common on the federal level, when that failed, we accepted the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That can be seen from the Cutileiro agreement, in all the other agreements, except the Vance-Owen Plan. We had all already agreed on everything. Momcilo Krajisnik, as a legalist, always insisted on the agreements that had been reached. We did not want to have a separate entity within Bosnia-Herzegovina. I loved the federal Yugoslavia, together with Slovenia, Croatia, and all the other republics. However, the system collapsed and we couldn't help it. Then our only choice was to do everything we could to prevent war. As for crimes, they say that I could have known about crimes, but let me assure you that I did not know of a single crime. Whenever some you report became available, the smallest indication -- I showed you that document. When Silajdzic told me back then at the airport that there were some girls captive in Foca, two of them were brought there and I was shocked to see them. One of them was pregnant; she was released immediately. The other one I took with me, to escort her. I would have punished every crime had I known about it. I have children of my own. Why on earth would I support criminals? No normal person in the world could have done that. They told me here that I was not a credible witness because I said I had never heard of Keraterm and Omarska at the time. I did not hear of the things that happened in Keraterm and Omarska. I heard them here for the first time, and I was shocked. It was terrible. I didn't know that such things could happen in our age. And that is the -- but then I didn't know about them, and that is the essence of the problem. Ethnic cleansing. Your Honours, I am not claiming there was no population movement. Of course. Serbs moved too. I know that I gave two statements, and I am one of those people who had to leave their home. I still dream of my home, of my birthplace. I would never wish it upon anyone, to experience what I experienced. And I believe those who went to investigate whether these things happened or not. Now, I believe that the great population movements happened. Destruction of religious buildings. I found a publication of the Serbian Orthodox church, and I tendered it to you, not as an attempt to prove that this didn't happen. But this war was going on, and it's incredible how all these churches and other religious monuments and buildings were destroyed, as if some evil spirit was released from the people, all of them. I know that enough evidence was placed before this Trial Chamber to completely refute the allegations of the Prosecution that I committed crimes or that I failed to prevent -- I failed to take measures to punish war crimes against Muslims and Croats during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I consider that enough proof was tendered that I made every effort to arrive at a just, political solution. It was demonstrated that the Serbian side did not advocate any solution which was outside the parameters of the position -- outside the parameters of the position taken by the international community. Throughout the war, at all times I was committed to an immediate cease-fire and withdrawal of Serbian forces from significant portions of territory, notwithstanding the fact that Serbs were owners of a proportionately greater percentage of BH territory than members of the other two communities. A large number of documents were tendered here that were not admitted into evidence. The claim that I testified untruthfully is completely unjustified. I never told untruths in my whole life, and I never told them here either. On every day of my testimony, I brought evidence to prove the veracity of what I had said the day before. Unfortunately, a lot of that evidence has not been admitted. I believe that the Trial Chamber has sufficient evidence to completely reject the charges of the Prosecution. I hope that that will be so, because any other decision would be contrary to truth and justice. Therefore, in the name of truth and justice, at the moment when the judgement in my case is close to being announced, I call upon any Muslims and Croats, if they have any evidence against me, to forward it to the Trial Chamber to consider it in its deliberations. I am not afraid of any new evidence because, although I am distressed by the realisation that crimes have been committed against innocent people in the course of the dreadful war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I remain serene because I am in a position to declare, before God and Your Honours, not only that I do not have a guilty conscience but that I am not guilty in relation to the charges pressed against me by the Prosecution. I hope that you will make a judgement in keeping with the truth and the documents. I want to thank you for your kindness to me over the past two and a half years. I hold nothing against the Prosecutors, because they were only doing their job. I have lost many friends, and everybody seems to have written me off. But I am certain that truth will prevail. I know, Your Honours, that you will make a just decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. This concludes this trial that started on the 3rd of February, 2004. On that day I said that the trial might keep us together for two years. It turned out to be now 31 months that we are together in this courtroom. The judgement will be delivered in due course, and the date of the delivery of the judgement will be announced in a scheduling order that the Chamber will issue as soon as it's able to do. We stand adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned sine die
